TextEng:
The following is a partial list of terms and phrases commonly used by Zhents of all walks of life in the post-Razing era. 

Artists: Wizards. 

The Charmer: Since Mystra's name is still a forbidden word, the citizens use this term instead. 

Converts: Zhentilar deserters who decided not to fight for Cyric during the Razing. 

The Eclipse: Derisive term for Cyric, the Dark Sun. Adopted when he failed to save the city during the Razing. 

The Flow: Casual name for the Tesh River.

Good News: Slang term for a supply caravan that has entered the city; used especially during the Horse Stew Days. 

Himself or Hisself: Lord Orgauth, former ruler of the Keep. Mostly used by the lower classes. Now more commonly used to refer to Fzoul.

Horse Stew Days: Called this because the citizens began stealing horses and eating them when food became scarce. See the Lean Months.
 
Innocents: Anyone who comes to Zhentil Keep unaware that it has been razed. 

To Kiss: To seduce information out of someone. 

The Lean Months: The three months following the siege, where supplies became extremely scarce. 

Mask: A scam. 

The Pile: The dump, located outside the city. 

The Razing: The destruction of most of Zhentil Keep by white dragons, frost giants, and humanoid armies. Also applies to the months of the siege that followed. 

The Rookery: Street nickname for the Citadel of the Raven. 

Sodchuckers: Dalesfolk. 

Take Out the Garbage: Kill someone and deposit the body in the dump. 

Zhentish Desserts: Gruesome nickname given to the frozen corpses that washed up during the siege after battles with the white dragons. 

Zhentish Handshake: Walking up to someone, whacking them upside the head with a club, and taking their goods.

To Zik: To stab.
A Guide to Zhentil Keep Slang

Dragoth the Bone Mage's master was Aumvor the Undying, an ancient Netherese lich, infamous since Netheril's Age of Discovery for his unmatched mastery over necromancy. He was named 'the Undying' because, instead of seeking lichdom, he lived for centuries by leeching the living energy of his 'living zombie' servitors, many of them members of his own family. He eventually transformed to a lich following the Fall of Netheril.

Created by following one of Aumvor's rituals in Dragoth Keep, this amulet grants various necromantic powers to its wearer.

Shadoweirs are as a type of religious knighthood of the woods who serve the goddess Mielikki. Its members are willing to go on the offensive on behalf of their sacred forests. They seek to advance the regrowth of ancient woodlands and halt the endless assault of civilization on their homelands.

The doppleganger Devalle presumably claimed this amulet from the hapless Shadoweir ranger whose form she took.

Carved in the shape of a wolf, this figure is magical, and rubbing it will summon a faithful dire wolf companion who can be summoned once per day to fight at your side. The wolf's name, "Cassius" is enscribed on the side of the figure.
This wooden figure is carved to resemble a dog or wolf. On the figure is inscribed the word "Cassius."
Astar's armor is superbly crafted and enchanted to ward off the strongest blows.
Lashan's father is exceptionally light and clings to you with all of his meager strength. The smell is overpowering.

Bone masks are fashioned of bone from any source. Greatly prized among the Zhentarim and other evil organizations that deal frequently with the undead, they both offer protection from and mastery over the dead.
When these sturdy bracers are knocked together in front of your chest, a magical shield quickly forms around you.
A key to the upper floor of the Breakwater Inn in Melvaunt.

This large book seems to be a journal of sorts. The final few pages are heavily scribbled with notes from the Bron's last meeting. Most of the notes are largely irrelevant, but a few catch your eye:

"... I need to replace that drunken lout Grimswold. Were he not mildly useful as a scapegoat should the need arise, I'd fire him immediately."

"... The Order attack on Teshwave has disrupted our food supplies. Voonlar can't afford to spare even a cup of grain. Things are going to get ugly before long."

"... Where's the damned backup Zhentil Keep was supposed to send? There are strange noises coming from beyond the town walls, and I'm starting to get nervous. I'm going to order the gates locked until reinforcements arrive."
These otherwise normal-looking bullets are enchanted to instantly expand in size upon striking a target, crushing them with the weight of a small boulder.
Originally a humble cheese knife, this blade has been repurposed into a thin, light dagger.

Cheswick's dagger is relatively plain except for the inscription on the blade itself, which reads: "Hidden but Never Unseen." What that means is anybody's guess.

Despite its unremarkable appearance, the dagger bears a strong enchantment. It grants its wielder the ability to polymorph for a short period of time. In addition, once per day, the wielder can see invisible creatures and objects as though they were in plain sight.

This rolled sheet of parchment is stamped with the official mark of the city of Hillsfar: a large, stylized "M" set in front of a pair of crossed blades.

The contract is only a few days old and makes for chilling reading. Zain, Raest and Thorn appear to have been hired by Maalthir, wizard ruler of Hillsfar, to spy on Voonlar and report back with news of any noteworthy events.

Most disturbingly, the contract also mentions a reward for the head of one Sharalyn Lockleaf, whom the contract calls a known Harper and an enemy of the city of Hillsfar.

You should let Sharalyn know of this failed attempt on her life.

The events of the recent conflict in Tethyr, during which the ogre mage warlord Sythillis marched an army of humanoids south into human lands, are still being picked over by sages and scholars from Candlekeep to Shadowdale. What triggered Sythillis to embark on a war with the powerful southern nation is still up for debate. What is known, however, is that many soldiers lost their lives in the brief conflict, which concluded in the elven city of Suldanessellar and an epic confrontation between the ogre warlord an unnamed hero. 

Though details are vague at this time, it appears that treachery was somehow afoot in the leadership of the Crimson Guard - the famed mercenary company hired by Queen Zaranda Star Rhindaun to defend Tethyr. One scholar speculates that the Crimson Guard intentionally instigated the conflict in order to win power in the kingdom. Another argues that a foul being known as a malaugrym was secretly behind the war, manipulating events for its own ends.

Regardless of the cause of the conflict, thousands died during an autumn that is already being referred to as the Bloody Fall. It is said the hero who eventually defeated Sythillis overcame slave traders, an imprisoned titan, and a horde of kobolds, ogres and worse during the desperate final battle for Suldanessellar. What became of him or her is unknown, and with events still so fresh, the veracity of the above will only be fully known in time - or to those fortunate enough to have witnessed them first-hand...
A cryptic message is written on this yellowed paper: 'To see, free a...'

The recent trouble in Daggerford, as with so many of the ills plaguing Faerûn, can be traced back to the Zhentarim. The suspicious death of Duke Pwyll Greatshout began a story of intrigue that ultimately resulted in a powerful devil named Gorgomorz being unleashed upon the Realms. Once again, in their quest to amass powerful and influence at any cost, the Black Network placed the lives of countless innocents in danger.

Fortunately, as is so often the case, a brave hero - or perhaps group of heroes, for the Dukes of Daggerford delight in recounting tales of their valor to any who will listen - came to the rescue. During the course of their adventures, our heroes are said to have resolved all manner problems experienced by the folk of the region, travelling from the Crab's Claw Coast to Trollbark Forest and even venturing down into the ancient ruins of Illefarn.

In the end, Gorgomorz himself was defeated inside Daggerford's very walls. The Zhentarim plot was exposed, and Greatshout himself was discovered alive and well. As with every story of such scope, however, there is much that must be left out in this brief telling. This humble author recommends that those seeking the thrills of high adventure get their hands upon a more comprehensive retelling of the period in which darkness lay over Daggerford...

Although it looks more like a large needle than an instrument of war, this dart has the deadly ability to hold a foe motionless. Targets struck by one of these darts risk being paralyzed as though by carrion crawler brain juice.

This enchanted chain mail armor is standard uniform for the Bron's deputies. When worn together with the helmet, it is doubtful a casual observer would be able to tell who is behind the armor. Unfortunately, the armor is only sized for a human or elf.
This helmet is part of the uniform that the Bron expects his deputies to wear at all times.

Forged by a Netherese Archwizard over two thousand years ago, this huge greatsword is one of the mightiest weapons of its type in Faerûn. 

Enchanted beyond the limits of what modern-day wizardry is able to achieve, Dominion's power can enslave the minds of humanoids and monsters alike. At the same time, the blade grants the wielder complete immunity to mind-affecting and death magic.

While Dominion is of little use in combat to those not accustomed to fighting with such weapons, its powers can be tapped by any being strong enough to command it.

One of the fabled Baneblades of Demron, Dragathil, like its sister blades, was forged in ancient Myth Drannor over the course of 300 years. Though the archmage Demron is credited with their creation, they were cooperative efforts among all the races that lived in Myth Drannor. As far as weapon collections go, they are unmatched in history of the Realms, with one exception - the Blades of Netheril.

Despite its fearsome power, Dragathil was designed to subdue opponents peacefully. Each of the Baneblades is keyed to a particular type of wielder: Dragathil can only be wielded by one of medium stature.
This large egg was given to you by Huntmaster Baerdeth Malagar of the Lodge of the Great Hunt in Zhentil Keep. You have no idea how he came to possess it.
Disputes between nobles are often resolved through duels which take place according to strict rules. Sometimes, however, a noble finds a way to cheat.

In the hands of a dwarf, this warhammer becomes a mighty weapon indeed. When hurled by a dwarf, the hammer inflicts 1d8 additional damage, or 2d8 additional damage against giants.

[Use Unique Power to hurl the hammer at the nearest enemy. It will instantly return.]
This large key opens to the gate leading east out of Voonlar.
Created by and for the Red Wizards and their agents, these black whips can daze a victim on a successful hit and bend them to the wielder's will.

Few places in the Moonsea can be considered peaceful and serene, but the ancient village of Elmwood is one of them. Elmwood is a farming community that supplements its income with a little fishing and woodcarving. Its location near the Dales and the former Elven Court has resulted in quite a bit of Dales blood and moon elf blood in the villagers, who have fond relationships with both of those communities. The old Moonsea saying "like an Elmwood watch" means a task so simple that it practically performs itself. This bit of lore bears testament to the reality that very little happens here.  

The village of Elmwood was established in the Year of the Screeching Vole, 163 DR, as a small waystation for ship traffic to and from the River Lis. Even back then it was a place of tranquility, where humans and elves could meet and interact on even terms. Elmwood managed to miss its share of dragon attacks and sacking armies, but it never grew into a town or city. The main reason for this was its lack of the natural resources most cities were founded to exploit: iron, gold, marble, granite, silver, and copper. Today, Elmwood does much of what it has always done: farming, fishing, and ferrying. Gods die, cities rise and fall, and Elmwood remains an oasis of calm in the midst of turmoil.

Elventree is a sylvan community established in 702 DR, the Year of the Dawn Rose, six years after the fall of Myth Drannor. This ancient settlement, a traditional meeting place for humans and elves, soon became a haven for half-elves, rangers, artists, and druids. It should come as no surprise to anyone that the community also soon became a Harper outpost. 

Elventree is not a typical Moonsea community. It is built in the traditional elven style of working in concert with nature. There are no cleared common grounds (other than natural clearings) or any large buildings. All structures in Elventree are located in either natural caverns or hollowed-out trees. There are no roads to speak of, only shady forest paths and almost-invisible trails that wind through the town. Elventree blends into the surrounding forest, and this has kept it safe for centuries.

A community of 200 elves, including women and children, calls Elventree home. These elves, mostly of wood elf stock, maintain close contact with others of their kind throughout Faerûn, and are looked upon as representatives of the Elven Court. The elves are friendly, but though they are active in the daily life of the town, they keep to themselves otherwise. Many are content to sing the old songs, tell the old tales, and carve things of beauty. On warm summer nights the air is filled with their clear voices, singing of the splendor of ancient Myth Drannor.

Eremuth's robe is of the finest quality, embodying the height of Waterdhavian fashion - around fifty years ago. Still, the strong enchantments weaved into the cloth more than compensates for its slightly outdated style. It's a miracle Eremuth hasn't been killed for having the audacity to wear such an outfit in the Moonsea...

This greatsword is identical in appearance to the real Dominion. A powerful item in its right, the mind-controlling magic bestowed by this sword is nonetheless a pale imitation of the original's. Still, the sword's magic was sufficient to fool Maganus, at least for a while.
A key to the upper floor of the Floating Fighter Inn in Melvaunt.

The blue sapphire is twin to the more precious ruby in all respects but color. In most stones, the sparkling blue color must be brought out by exposure to great heat. Once "cooked," the color change is permanent and does not otherwise affect the much-treasured durability of the gem.

The particular specimen is of huge size and likely worth a considerable amount of gold.

This blood-red sword seems to hum with evil energy, hungering after victims to feed upon. Whenever you stare at it for any length of time, the image of a narrow-faced, grinning man seems to force itself into your brain. There is something very wrong with this weapon, and its presence in an unremarkable smith seems eerily like divine providence...
This magic armor grants additional protection to its wearer, but it doesn't bear the hallmarks of any specific maker.

TextEng: The Hammer of Vorbyx is named after its last owner, an ogre king who ruled Thar. However, Vorbyx allegedly plundered the weapon from an ancient unmarked barrow, so its true origins are lost in time. More than a mere scepter, it served as a symbol of Vorbyx's authority over the unruly ogre and orc tribes of Thar, and when he died without a worthy successor, his most loyal followers buried the weapon with him, believing that he would need it to wage wars in the afterlife.

Seek out a man named Jeffers in the Zhents' Quarter in Mulmaster. I understand he knows more of this "Maganus" you seek.

Needless to say, if you approach me with this note, I will deny all knowledge of it.

- K.

Harper pins are silver brooches given to new members of the Harpers. They protect the wearer from various spells designed to read a person's thoughts.

Undercover Harper agents often use these pins to identify each other when operating in places their presence would not be tolerated.

You should hold on to this item in case it is needed to persuade certain characters to talk.

This bow radiates a strong glow. It seems so perfect as to be impossible to achieve with mortal materials in the hands of a mortal bowyer. It is therefore likely the bow originated in the Upper Planes, and was perhaps the favored weapon of a powerful angel or the exarch of some benevolent deity.

These swords are forged from an ore found only on the deepest layers of the Abyss, and are possessed only by the most powerful and influential demons, such as great balor generals.

The sword retains its connection to the place from which it originated. Even after thousands of years and through multiple planes of existence, the sword's ties to the Outer Plane remain strong.
The fabled helm of Balduran, legendary founder of Baldur's Gate, has long been rumored to wield powerful protective magic. The exact nature of this magic, however, has not yet been determined.
Hilrad's White Robe of the Archmagi

Prized for their vibrant green color, emeralds are fragile and need to be protected from the impacts and extreme temperature changes common to adventuring life. It is a highly prized gem by the wealthy and royalty alike.

This particular specimen is of huge size and likely terrific value.

Bright and beautiful, the ruby is famous for its clear and bloody hue. To some it is the gem of love, to others the gem of revenge. To all it is unquestionably precious, and the largest, most flawless specimens are more highly prized than diamonds. The goddess Sune is said to sometimes wear rubies in her wild hair.

This particular specimen is of huge size and surely of great value.

The blue sapphire is twin to the more precious ruby in all respects but color. In most stones, the sparkling blue color must be brought out by exposure to great heat. Once "cooked," the color change is permanent and does not otherwise affect the much-treasured durability of the gem.

The particular specimen is of huge size and likely worth a considerable amount of gold.

Best known in its pale, orange-yellow form, topaz is an attractive gem that appears in well-formed, multifaceted crystals. These crystals can reach an incredible size, and specimens weighing several hundred pounds are not unknown. The largest stones are customarily reserved for gifts on state occasions, and only the greatest master gemcutters are allowed to work them.

This particular specimen is of huge size and would likely fetch a decent sum of gold.
Enchanted by old Elven magic, these small red berries have a very minor restorative power.
These small round red berries are unusually firm.
Arsenic Poison. Initial Save DC: 13 Initial Effect: Lowers CON by 1. Secondary Effect: Lowers CON by 2D8.
Black Lotus Extract Poison. Initial Save DC: 20 Initial Effect: Lowers CON by 3D6. Secondary Effect: Lowers CON by 3D6.
Bloodroot Poison. Initial Save DC: 12 Initial Effect: Lowers WIS by 1D3. Secondary Effect: Lowers CON by 1D4.
Greenblood Oil Poison. Initial Save DC: 13 Initial Effect: Lowers CON by 1. Secondary Effect: Lowers CON by 1D2.
Id Moss Poison. Initial Save DC: 14 Initial Effect: Lowers INT by 1D4. Secondary Effect: Lowers INT by 2D6.
Malyss Root Paste Poison. Initial Save DC: 16 Initial Effect: Lowers DEX by 1. Secondary Effect: Lowers DEX by 2D4.
Nitharit Poison. Initial Save DC: 13 Initial Effect: Nothing. Secondary Effect: Lowers CON by 3D6.
Sassone Leaf Residue Poison. Initial Save DC: 16 Initial Effect: 2D12 Acid damage. Secondary Effect: Lowers CON by 1D6.
Oil of Taggit Poison. Initial Save DC: 15 Initial Effect: Nothing. Secondary Effect: Puts target to sleep for 10 rounds.
Terinav Root Poison. Initial Save DC: 16 Initial Effect: Lowers DEX by 1D6. Secondary Effect: Lowers DEX by 2D6.
Striped Toadstool Poison. Initial Save DC: 11 Initial Effect: Lowers WIS by 1. Secondary Effect: Lowers WIS by 2D6.
The word "Lita" is engraved on the side of this shiny silver ring.

This wedding band is enchanted with powerful magic to keep the wearer safe from fear and mind-affecting spells, as well as poison. It is therefore a ring perfectly suited to those who move in circles where skullduggery is a fact of life.

Engraved on the inside of the band is "Astar."
This is the key Sharalyn gave you. It unlocks the door leading to the upper floor of the Swords' Meet Inn.

This axe once belonged to the dwarven hero, Dorgan Orcsmasher. The Orcsmasher clan was famed for its hatred of orcs and goblinkind, and for many centuries was the bane of the evil humanoids living in the Cloud Peak Mountains.

One dark morning an alliance of orcs and goblins swept down out of the mountains and invaded the Orcsmasher clan home. Following several days of terrible fighting, only Dorgan and his wife and children remained from the original century of dwarves that once made up clan Orcsmasher. 

Urging his family to flee, Dorgan stood alone against the advancing horde, like an immovable oak. Time and time again he threw back the humanoids, deflecting countless attacks with his mighty axe and shrugging off wounds that would have killed many a dwarf outright. 

Dorgan's family managed to escape thanks to his heroics. Upon returning to the clan home a year later, they found the fallen dwarf propped up against a mountain of orcs and goblins. On the floor, they found his axe. Dorgan's name is celebrated amongst his kind as an example of the tenacity and endurance possessed by the dwarven race.

So named for the small ruby resembling an eye at its center, this buckler's magic grants greater protection than its appearance would suggest. The shield's true power manifests when its user is struck in combat, channeling their pain and deflecting it back upon their attacker. While this causes no physical damage, the target is overcome with an overwhelming fear of death. This heightened sense of mortality can often prove detrimental to the attacker.

"Grimswold,

Due to your habit of getting drunk at the Meet and forgetting to lock your door, I've decided to take away your key. It wouldn't do to have some nosy adventurer stumble across it and attempt to infiltrate the Locktower.

Be grateful that I haven't thrown you in the cells for gross negligence, and know that I only retain your services because your unique brand of incompetence makes us all look good by comparison.

And, for Bane's sake man, remember to don your armor before returning to the Locktower! We won't let you in otherwise. We can't take unnecessary risks in these dark times. There are spies and agents everywhere.

- the Bron"

This black, leather-bound journal appears to have once belonged to Voonlar's high priest of Bane, Gormstadd, before his death. The journal recounts the priest's efforts to raise an undead army from the buried remains entombed within the catacombs beneath Voonlar.

=======================
Entry 1
=======================

Word has just arrived from Zhentil Keep - from Lord Fzoul himself, no less. He has instructed me to raise an undead army for deployment against the Order of the Crippled Fang. Alas, I fear Fzoul overestimates the power of the clergy here in Voonlar. Only Merkul and Charon possess sufficient experience to assist me in the ancient rituals for raising the dead.

=======================
Entry 2
=======================

Those Chaunteans continue to frustrate me! I dearly wish to see Shrae beheaded and the Earthmother's temple razed to the ground. However, despite my best efforts, I still do not have sufficient justification to move against them. I am unwilling to draw the wrath of Shadowdale or the Harpers by acting precipitously.
 
But enough about those do-gooding fools. Something unexpected occurred today. Charon claims to have received telepathic contact from a mysterious being whilst exploring the darkest reaches of the catacombs. Upon further investigation, we found a sealed door besides an ancient stone pillar etched with scenes glorifying the Black Lord Bane. No more communication was forthcoming, so I will try again on the morrow.

=======================
Entry 3
=======================

The mysterious entity today revealed itself to me. His name is Shrazgul, and he claims to have once been a powerful priest of Bane before he was eventually rewarded with eternal life. I have heard of such beings -- baneliches they are called, the result of the Black Lord's greatest blessing.

I believe I have discovered a powerful ally, although Shrazgul's intentions are still unclear. He has asked me to recover four missing pieces of Bane's symbol, which will enable the magically sealed door to open. I will do as he requested. I do not fear Shrazgul, for we serve the same lord, do we not?

=======================
Entry 4
=======================

I managed to recover the pieces of the missing symbol, which were scattered around the furthest reaches of the catacombs, and gain access to Shrazgul's resting place. He is magnificent to behold, a festering visage of dread and terror made real. Someone must have imprisoned the banelich beneath Voonlar, although it makes no sense for such a revered servant of the Black Lord to be imprisoned directly beneath one of his temples.

I searched the ancient texts and journals in the temple for clues, but all mentions of Shrazgul seem to have been erased. The banelich would not answer my questions regarding his imprisonment, but he did lend his assistance raising corpses in the catacombs to do my bidding. This is a boon indeed!

=======================
Entry 5
=======================

I am beginning to realize that something is terribly amiss with my new ally. Shrazgul seeks more control over the undead that I am happy to permit, and I am helpless to deny his power. He is possessed of unimaginable arrogance, bordering on blasphemy. Is it possible Shrazgul was bound there by the priesthood of the Black Lord as penance for past sins?

=======================
Entry 6
=======================

I have been betrayed! The undead horde I spent these last few months amassing has turned against me! Shrazgul was behind it all. I fear he is no longer a servant of Bane's will. No, the banelich has its own agenda. To make matters worse, Merkul and Charon were slain by the very dead they helped animate. I saw them torn apart by jagged claw and broken fang. At least their deaths warned me of Shrazgul's betrayal before I suffered the same fate.

I managed to steal the fourth piece of the symbol before fleeing the catacombs, sealing the banelich in his chamber once again. The remaining three pieces are still down there. No doubt Shrazgul will send his minions to recover the last quadrant. They are slow and cumbersome, but eventually they will discover the entrance to the surface.

The Zhentarim representatives in the town have assured me that reinforcements are on their way from Zhentil Keep. Until then, Voonlar is woefully unprepared in the event of an Order attack.

This is the final entry in the journal. The ink still looks fresh.

This ancient and terrible weapon was presumed lost to the Realms when the banelich Shrazgul disappeared in 1135 DR.

Shrazgul was infamous for wielding this weapon with abandon, even employing it against fellow worshippers of Bane when he judged them guilty of some supposed slight against him.

The wicked head of the flail can smash through bone with ease. Shrazgul named the weapon "The Black Lord's Caress" in a supposed act of piety towards his deity. Alas, that wasn't enough to stop Bane from imprisoning his wayward priest when he became too difficult to control.
This large key was found on the body of the frost giant jarl, Bashnagg.

This spear was used by the frost giant Agatha to almost instantly heat the huge cauldron she used to feed her clan. In Agatha's giant fists, it was less a spear and more an implement supreme culinary efficiency.
This great axe was until recently the famed weapon of the fearsome Red Minotaur, champion of Hillsfar's arena. It seems someone claimed it from the fallen minotaur and sold it on to a merchant.

This appears to be Eremuth's journal, dating back months before he met you at the Swords' Meet Inn. You flick through and note the most interesting entries.

=======================
Entry 1
=======================

I grow tired of Waterdeep. My mother forbids me from devouring the mages and nobles of the city and I grow weary of feeding on beggars and unsuspecting adventurers. Fortunately, she is soon to reveal the "great scheme" the Unseen has been plotting. For her sake, I hope it piques my interest. I acknowledge my mother's usefulness in birthing me, but I find my mind wandering often to how it would feel to murder her when she least suspects it...

=======================
Entry 2
=======================

Finally, the Unseen have contacted me! Hlaavin himself told me of the organization's plans to seize power in Melvaunt. First, I am to establish a base in Elmwood, where the simpletons of the backwater town will never suspect a thing.

Hlaavin spoke of another matter, one I find of more interest than the doppelganger's dull political ambitions. A human archmage of note recently dug up one of the legendary Blades of Netheril. The ragtag cult he formed is hiding out somewhere in the Moonsea region.

=======================
Entry 3
=======================

That fool Hlaavin saw the merit in my plan to retrieve the Netherese artifact. I shall need help, for even with my vast powers, I am but one. My worthless sister refused her help in this matter, so I will need to find some gullible fools to help me get my hands on the blade. I will head west to Voonlar. The Zhentarim are incompetent fools, but heroes often travel north from Shadowdale, the home of our most hated enemy, and would make a good target for my manipulations. One day I will stick Elminster's head on a spike, damn him...

My lair in Elmwood is most agreeable. An ancient and vast colony of spiders has dwelled within the darkness of these tunnels for centuries. I see them scuttling high above, but they leave me well alone, for my true form is as alien to them as they are to most human fools. I am certain my wretched sister would be pleased to learn of their presence. Spiders always did fascinate her.

=======================
Entry 4
=======================

This is my first entry in a while. It is difficult to find the focus to write when one is constantly keeping tabs on braindead adventurers and their band of misfit henchmen. As it happens, the dupe I chose at least proved competent and was able to overcome the cult. Dominion will soon be mine! I merely need wait for the opportune moment...

=======================
Entry 5
=======================

Success! Dominion is mine! I killed the human Astar during my grand betrayal, an act that pleased me greatly. He was so very boring. 

Alas, the hunger I had suppressed since Voonlar grew too much, and I succumbed to temptation upon returning to my lair here in Elmwood. The druid and the girl were both delicious. I may kill once more before I depart to report my success to my sister and our Unseen contact in Hillsfar. We are to meet at a place called Laris's Curios, before joining the rest of the cell in Melvaunt.

Who to eat before I depart? The lovely priestess at the temple or the human male who runs the inn? Devalle has her eye on him - if she devours his brain before I can suck out his insides, I shall be most distraught. 

=======================
Entry 6
=======================

The "hero" I tricked into helping me retrieve Dominion has followed me here! Damn them. I will send word to Sorin and Devalle and then make plans to put an end to their meddling once and for all. I only hope the archmage Maganus does not discover my whereabouts, for he will be a more difficult obstacle to deal with.

This letter is addressed to a woman named Lana. The faded ink reveals the letter to have been written some time ago.

"Where do I begin? I should have sent this letter after I left Mulmaster. A tenday turned into a month, and then a month turned into a year, and then a decade. There is no excuse, except to say that I feared hurting you. The real truth, however, is that I am a coward.

I was given no choice but to flee Mulmaster. I did not even have time to stop and warn you, for your own life was in danger every second I remained in the city. I could not follow through with Selfaril's orders to assassinate the young noblewoman: this much you knew. 

What you did not know, however, was that she and I were having an affair.

I swear to you, Lana - the brief relationship we had, though a cruel betrayal of our own vows, did not influence my decision to refuse Selfaril's orders. I am a coward and unfaithful, but I am no murderer of innocents. Even as you read this, even despite the hatred you must surely feel for me, I trust you know this much to be true.

I am so sorry, Lana. Even had I the time to warn you, I would not have had you abandon your life in Mulmaster. You deserved better than to throw away everything we had worked so hard for. You deserved better than to abandon a life of hard-won luxury for an uncertain future with a man who could not be true to you. I pray that you have found happiness in the years since. I pray that you found a good man; an honest man. One whose skills extend beyond his sword-arm. 

I loved you, Lana. For all of my failings, I want you to know this. The years we spent together were the best of my life. How I wish things had turned out differently.

"That which should not be alive shall die" is the philosophy behind this powerful club. Against such unnatural foes, the club inflicts tremendous damage.

These powerful flails are often employed by clerics of Tempus and other war-focused gods, who love nothing more than to wade into battle crying their deity's name and fighting enemy warriors head-on. Often the fight is over before it has even begun, as the unsuspecting warriors find themselves scrabbling desperately in the mud for their weapons while the cleric in possession of one these fails readies the killing blow.

Hlessen Muragh of the Purple Portals in Melvaunt is one of the foremost artificers in the Realms. As a self-proclaimed golem aficionado, he often finds it necessary to deconstruct his creations as quickly and painlessly as possible. This hammer was created for just such a purpose.

This simple-looking axe was apparently named after a warrior who called himself the Wolf. Despite its basic appearance, the axe bestows complete immunity to death fear and mind-affecting spells upon the wielder, making them a grim and unshakeable force of single-minded fury.

This deadly scythe carries a little of the essence of the dead God of the Dead, Myrkul. The one wielding the scythe allows this essence inside them and becomes a walking dealer of death, at the cost of ignoring their own well-being.

This the journal of Dragoth the Bone Mage. It chronicles much of his life: from his childhood, to his years apprenticed to an ancient wizard known as the Undying, and then the decades he spent in Suzail, capital of Cormyr, where he secretly experimented on the dead. Lyressa features prominently, for it transpires she and Dragoth were lovers. Lyressa was one of the city's most infamous thieves when she met Dragoth, but under his influence she soon began to learn the darker arts of murder, in order to procure Dragoth new bodies upon which to experiment.

The journal entries become increasingly melancholy as Dragoth writes of Lyressa's desire for a child, and the toxins he secretly slipped into her drink to ensure this would not come to pass. Their relationship soured, until one night they argued, and he mortally wounded her. Thinking to save her, he performed a ritual his master the Undying had taught him. It backfired and instead of becoming a living zombie, as Dragoth had intended, Lyressa became a true zombie. She remained inert for years, trapped in a stasis spell Dragoth placed upon her to stop her body decaying. Until one day she awoke, remembering nothing, and fled Suzail.

Dragoth appears to have lived a lonely and wretched existence since that time, shunning the company of the undead for the living. It would appear he moved to Thentia earnestly seeking the company of his peers in Firefingers, and the other retired archmages of the city. He kept Lyressa's sword and shield, evil weapons that without her assassin training, she would not be able to utilize. It appears his motivations were simply to have something to remember her by.

This journal belongs to the young nobleman Bale Khodolos. It recounts his search for the legendary Bright Sword of Thentia. Reading the journal, you learn that Bale discovered the blade, which he refers to as "Beirmoura," several tendays past. At first, he was delighted - with the sentient weapon guiding his arm, he was able to vanquish his rival, Gideon, in a duel that won him the admiration of many young noblewomen. 

Beirmoura's irritation at this development was the first sign of what would follow.

The Bright Sword's ego proved too much for Bale to handle. In addition to being bloodthirsty and impulsive, Bale claims that Beirmoura is slowly taking control of his thoughts and deeds. In particular, the sentient weapon has become obsessed with slaying the Netherese search party that is excavating the nearby ruins.

Bale fears that if he cannot rid himself of the sword soon, he will inadvertently lead himself and his comrades to an unfortunate end. Try as he might, however, he cannot part with the weapon. He is now a slave to Beirmoura's will, a fact of which none of his fellow nobles are aware.

After hurrying from the room, slipping and sliding on their own blood, the former Loviatans immediately denounced their faith and joined the church of Ilmater.

Also known as a "Mage-Killer," these shields are typically used by the most skilled mercenaries and assassins when tasked with hunting down a particularly troublesome mage. Even good wizards such as Elminster of Shadowdale and Khelben of Waterdeep possess a healthy dislike of these items, though common folk can often be heard saying, usually quietly, that they merely level the field.

Created deep within the experimental laboratories of Darkhold, the Render is without doubt one of the most savage creatures to ever walk the face of Faerûn. 

The creation of the Render was a terrible accident. The beast is an unholy combination of a summoned tanar'ri and a human prisoner of the Zhentarim. While nefariously allowing the tanar'ri to kill a prisoner for pleasure, a Zhentarim wizard miscast an unknown spell from a scroll. The spell killed the wizard and joined together the tanar'ri and the dying human. The resulting creature killed hundreds of Zhents in Darkhold before escaping into the Far Hills to the south of the citadel, where it has hunted ever since. The render has no memory of its former lives. As far as it is concerned, its existence began in the dungeons of Darkhold. 

The creature is in constant pain from its unholy union. The only way it knows to temporarily relieve this pain is to kill and consume prey - thus the render is a constantly active eating machine. Since the creature fears nothing, it is truly deadly. The render's greatest advantage is its ability to regenerate in a manner similar to a troll. Only electrical damage can permanently kill the render. 

The Zhentarim are desperate to capture the render, but all attempts to do so thus far by Zhentarim wizards and Zhentilar troops have caused twoscore casualties and met with no success.

The infinitely deep Abyss is the realm of both chaos and evil - the primary demesne of demons. Each of its infinite layers holds a different sort of inhospitable environment - swamps of fire, mountains of ice, crushing caverns, and empty voids. 
Individual demons have, over the course of millennia, risen from the hordes of their brethren. They gained great power and authority, then established themselves as demon lords. A few demon lords have even risen above the other demon lords, calling themselves demon princes.

These are all self-proclaimed titles. There are no actual qualifications; the Abyss is far too chaotic to develop rigid standards. It is this chaos and lack of organization and hierarchy that separates the demon lords from the archdevils, who have a rigid pecking order, each paying fealty to those in more powerful positions.

Almost every demon lord controls at least one layer of the Abyss. The lords command palaces and fortresses full of lesser demons and monsters, often decorated with tortured prisoners or tormented, damned souls. The demon lords relish pain and suffering as much as they lust for power. They savor corruption and destruction, waging eternal wars with each other to gain dominance. For many years, Demogorgon has been the most powerful demon lord, calling himself Prince of Demons. Both Orcus and Graz'zt contest this title, however. 

Many demon lords, and all demon princes, have a scattering of mortal worshipers gathered in secret cults. These demon cultists may one day, through their sacrifices and devotion, elevate the lords to true godhood, a title that many of the lords, particularly Orcus, have claimed at one time or another.

Iyrauroth, also called "the Wyrm of the Peaks," is a male great wyrm black dragon that has laired in the steppes of Thar and in Mount Grimmerfang in the Vast.

In fear of his older sister, Embrurshaile, Iyrauroth spent centuries of his life hiding on other continents. During this time, he sired sixteen sons and daughters. Embrurshaile's death caused a magical backlash in the Weave that likely notified her brother of her demise. He immediately set off with his children to conquer her territory in the Galena Mountains and Thar, joining the Dark Alliance in the process and helping to lay waste to Northkeep in the Year of the Blue Shield, 400 DR. He later went on to destroy Tharniir, shattering the power of the ogres of Thar.

In the Year of Writhing Darkness, 572 DR, Iyrauroth killed with claw and fang the orc Ologh, the Overking of Vastar, plunging the orcish kingdom into civil war.

Iyrauroth later fell into a deep slumber under the steppes of Thar that lasted for centuries.

A Cult of the Dragon cell, namely the Wyrmsmoke cell, awoke Iyrauroth by 1369 DR. They attempted to persuade him to undergo the transformation into a dracolich, and gave him offerings. Iyrauroth only found their efforts amusing.

Stirred from his rest now, Iyrauroth acted as he pleased, and took to raiding caravans crossing Thar between Glister, Melvaunt, and Phlan, including those run by the Cult. When a whole caravan to Glister disappeared and agents reported on the previously unknown black dragon's raids, the Zhentarim feared that the Cult of the Dragon was responsible. To preserve trade, they marched Zhentilar troops into Thar, to which the Cult reacted by rallying local tribes to their cause, until a war loomed.

Iyrauroth's current whereabouts and activities are unknown. What is certain, however, is that the Wyrm of the Peaks remains one of the most dangerous black dragons to have plagued the northern Realms.
Iyrauroth: The Wyrm of the Peaks

This large, leather-bound journal appears to have belonged to Maganus. Somewhat surprisingly, the book is not magically warded - though it is unlikely the archmage would ever have conceived of someone penetrating his inner sanctum. The journal details the major events of his life over the last few years, beginning with his recovery of the Netherese artifact Dominion from the Great Glacier.

Throughout the journal, Maganus's regret at his actions is obvious. It is clear that he is a man who knows the evil of what it is he does but is nonetheless committed to his course of action. From first contacting the Crippled Fang, to his alliance with the ogre mages of Kur-Tharsu, the archmage writes of how, in another life and another time, he might have been the one to stand in their way.

There is another noticeable theme besides his guilt at his actions, which is that Maganus is afraid. He makes frequent reference to a bargain he made with a demon prince on the morning he was supposed to hang on the walls of Zhentil Keep. He lost an eye that day - but his life was saved by the intervention of a force greater even than the Zhentarim. In return for saving Maganus so that he might finish his crusade against the Black Network, this demon prince was promised the archmage's everlasting soul. The final line of the journal is telling:

"I do not fear death," Maganus writes. "I fear what comes after."

In all the history of the civilized races, no nation forwarded the advancement of magic so much, or fell so quickly, as the human nation of Netheril. Ruled by Archwizards whose power was so great they created flying cities in the clouds, Netheril remains the ultimate testament both to human ambition and human hubris. 

It is said that the mightiest Archwizards of Netheril could challenge the very gods, and in the end, this proved to be their undoing. The Archwizard Karsus, desperately seeking a way to fight back against the magic-draining race known as the phaerimm which were threatening the existence of Netheril, cast a mighty spell that stole the divinity of the goddess of magic. Unable to cope with his sudden ascent to godhood, Karsus was destroyed by the divine energy tearing him apart. In an instant, magic failed across the Realms. The floating enclaves of Netheril fell and crashed to earth, killing all within.

Even now, almost two thousand years after the Fall of Netheril, remnants of that great civilization remain to remind us of an age when magic was at its zenith. Among the most powerful artifacts of ancient Netheril were the Blades, each one forged by one of the greatest Archwizards of the period. It is said that with such a weapon, one of ambition could raise or destroy armies, for they each hold a portion of their creator's power. Fortunately, all such weapons have been lost. For the sake of continued peace in the Realms, it might be best for all  if they rest undiscovered until the end of time.
Netheril: The Pride of the Archwizards

Also known as the Great Gray Land, Thar is a windswept, broken moor with a harsh climate. The local ogres and orcs speak of a time when their people built a great kingdom here, but nothing is left of it now except warring tribes. Legends also speak of Vorbyx's Hammer, a great weapon carried by the first king of Thar, which is presumably hidden somewhere waiting for a new king to wield it. Manticores, giant lizards, bulettes, and flying monstrosities such as yrthaks roam the land. The region is used as a caravan route through the northern Moonsea, with the trademeet site of Glister being the sole human settlement in the area.

The many humanoid tribes of Thar often carry out attacks on caravans heading to or from Glister, the camps in the Galenas foothills, or villages in the Stojanow Vale. In an attempt to keep them in check and bring stability to the area, lords and merchants have been known to enter into agreements with the tribes to encourage them not to attack, but these agreements break down easily. Scouts, hired adventuring companies, and the barbarians of the Ride also venture into Thar to hunt these tribes and destroy any creatures they encounter.

Of old, the lands north of the Moonsea coast were what human chroniclers call "the Land of the Beast-Men," or "the great gray land of Thar."

Thar is a land of gray stone, tumbled boulders, and loose scree heaped and scattered everywhere across open wilderland. Rolling hills are split here and there by sharp, sinuous stony ridges "like the tails of gigantic dragons frozen forever in stone," as the human sage Gharoanrus of Tsurlagol put it.

In the days before the rise of Zhentil Keep, this region was "a-crawl with orcs," being the northernmost reach of the orc realm of Vastar, but before that it was a kingdom of the beast-men, or ogres and before that, a realm of giants.

A succession of Tharkuls ruled the ogre kingdom of Thar, and they wielded a great hammer that only a large and strong ogre could hope to swing. No ogre could be Tharkul without the hammer, but no ogre could hold the Tharkul-seat for long without the respect of the ogre elders and many would-be usurpers always lurked, for the Tortured Lands were near at hand. That difficult terrain of stone needles, upthrust from the rock like the bristles of a thistle, offered hiding for hundreds of hardy creatures. Caves riddled the area, with ice in the deep and shadowed places. Here, cold-tolerating creatures served as ready food, from small birds to large stalking and slithering monsters.

Many Tharkuls fell in battle or died of the wounds they took when defeating a challenge from another ogre seeking to be Tharkul. A few succumbed to disease or the ravages of advanced age and died as sitting Tharkuls.

Unknown to most, the true power behind the Tharkuls lay in the Kur-Tharsu, or "Overlords of Thar." These ogres - commonly called oni in western Faerûn, though in truth they are but the weakest form of the formidable oni that originated in Kara-Tur - built a great stronghold from which they ruled over their kingdom and manipulated the current Tharkul. It is said the great gate of the Kur-Tharsu stronghold is impenetrable, and that it is large enough to house an army capable of overrunning a human city.

The foul malaugrym were until recently thought to be the corrupt and tainted offspring of the wizard Malaug, reputedly the first human to explore the Plane of Shadow, preceding even the Netherese. However, that theory may have been incorrect, for the vile clan of shapeshifting creatures may have originated in a place even more alien than the Plane of Shadow.

Able to duplicate any creature that it has ever seen with near perfection, each malaugrym nevertheless has one favorite form that it reverts to when seriously threatened. Normally, however, the malaugrym blend into the population of Faerûn, masquerading as humanoids and settling for periods of time in great urban centers where their favorite food - humans - is plentiful.

The malaugrym eventually plan to invade Faerûn but are hindered by several weaknesses, including an inability to master planar magic and a pathological need to amuse themselves with acts of cruelty. The leader of the race is known as the Shadowmaster, and the creatures are collectively known as the shadowmasters. Until recently, five of these creatures were known to inhabit Faerûn. The last couple of years, however, has seen a near doubling of that number. Should the malaugrym ever make a concerted effort to work together, rather than pursuing their own individual agendas, the Realms could quickly face a threat of epic proportions.

What the typical Faerûnian scholar understands to be an oni - an ogre mage - is but a weaker variety of the oni that inhabit the eastern lands of Kara-Tur. Violent creatures of great strength and even greater magical abilities, the mightiest oni rival the greatest demons and genies in power. This katana was created by one such being, perhaps with ideas of conquering the western lands in mind.

There is something odd about this weapon - its powers are nowhere near as strong as you remember. It is as though someone drained Dominion of much of its power, or else created a convincing duplicate of the real weapon. What reason anyone would have to do that, however, you have no idea.

Lyressa's tunic is a dark, midnight blue and black, ideal for blending into the shadows during the early hours of the morning. It smells faintly of herbs, which Lyressa employs to keep herself smelling "fresh".

Armor made from the scales of evil chromatic dragons are uncommon, but this armor was made from the scales of a dead gold dragon - a paragon of good. Given its presence among Iyrauroth's hoard, it is reasonable to assume the Wyrm of the Peaks had a hand, or rather a claw, in its creation. However it came to be, the armor is incredibly light and strong, able to turn away the mightiest of blows.

These weapons are used by many evil priests and warriors across the Realms. These metal maces are fearsomely spiked and allow the wielder to create darkness at will. Only evil beings may use these weapons: if they touch the flesh of a good-aligned creature, they immediately deal a powerful electrical shock.

Blessed under the light of the full moon by a high-ranking priest of Selûne, these maces are particularly effective against the undead who wither from the divine moonlight stored within the mace's sharp flanges. This lunar power also imparts the wielder with restorative abilities in order to heal the afflicted.

Oh, mighty Wyrm of the Peaks, whose name we are not worthy to utter, we hope this message reaches your magnificent, maleficent self, and that the messenger who delivered it proved to be a satisfying meal for your voracious appetite.

How we long to see you soaring above us, your wings darkening the sky, as you breathe your acidic elixir upon those who do not bow before your undoubted might.

We have established a base in Thentia, and even from this distance we can detect the unmistakable power of your aura, which we bask in with humble gratitude every moment of the day.

Our servitude is eternal and unquestionable, and we remain willing to provide our humble assistance if you choose to accept our offer of conducting the transformation process. 

Already we have commenced procuring the artefacts necessary to complete the ceremony, and we tremble with anticipation at the thought of the most powerful dragon in the Realms becoming a dracolich!

Your power is indisputable and unrivaled, yet this metamorphosis would ensure deserved immortality for the greatest dragon there ever has been, or will be!

Your servant,

The true name of this terrible spear has been lost through time, but those souls lucky enough to have survived an encounter with the Dark Druids of the Archwood have taken to referring to it simply as "Pigsticker." Unlike most druids, the Dark Druids of the Archwood make effort to accommodate the needs of civilization. Woodcutters and hunters who are foolish enough to enter the forest run the risk of an encounter with these evil druids, who deal slay without mercy.

Necromancers have very little tolerance for jokes at their expense, so the reaction of Lord Agorn Deathknell to a precariously perched bucket of chum above his laboratory door was entirely predictable, as was the death of the pixie responsible. The surprising part, especially to Argon, was the retaliation of dozens of outraged fey folk, who never suffer a poor sport. A number of their blades were recovered from Agorn's carcass.
These powerful potions imbue the drinker with great strength and fortitude.
This rusty old key unlocks the gate leading down to the prison beneath the Locktower.

This short sword is likely of drow origin. Scholars have translated the name to mean "Eater of Souls," and that seems appropriate: the sword feasts on the life of those it wounds, transferring some of this energy back to its wielder. Lyressa will not elaborate on how she originally came by the weapon, but its power is eminently suited to her undead state and new-found assassination skills.
This key was created from some reddish metal and is curiously warm to the touch.

The common faiths of the Moonsea reflect its dangerous nature; most of the gods worshiped here are of the "worship me or bad things will happen to you" variety, and the rest fall into the "worship me or I will do bad things to you" category. Whether overt or subtle, these faiths influence how the local people think. Visitors who worship bright and noble gods are likely to be scoffed at behind their backs, while those who worship "frivolous" deities such as Eldath, Lliira, Milil, Sharess, and Sune are often derided to their face. Adventurers who proselytize "foreign" religions quickly draw the attention of Banite loyalists and others who openly serve the evil deities favored here. Most Moonsea folk pay lip service to these deities just to keep potential threats away, not necessarily fully embracing the dark philosophies of these deities.
This light crossbow has been specially enchanted so that it can fire and reload much faster than a regular crossbow. As a side effect, it also greatly increases the movement speed of the wielder.

These powerful rings can neutralize any known poison. They are highly prized among members of the Black Network, who are no strangers to using underhanded methods like poisoning their rivals to get ahead.
This key is worn and rusty with age, but still appears to be functional.

That's it, we're done here. This damned warehouse is haunted.

- Baz

To free someone from the Imprisonment spell, you must cast this spell at the spot where he or she was entombed.

This scroll, given to you by Sharalyn Lockleaf, casts a spell of illusion upon you, allowing you to pass as human while in Hillsfar. The effects are only temporary, and the scroll has but a single use. You should wait until you are within sight of Hillsfar's walls before using it.

The legendary Tharkul, Halangarog the Four-Armed, is infamous for being the only Tharkul to walk away from Thar. Unlike every other Tharkul, he was never vanquished in battle or died of age old: he simply decided he had had enough. 

The Seven Stars were gifts from Halangarog's seven oni advisors before he relinquished the throne, for they were impressed with Tharkul's mastery of the eastern weapons. Each of the ogre mages imparted a little of their life force into their star, hoping to see them one day used in battle. Alas, Halangarog abdicated before it ever came to pass.

This shard of glass was taken from the shattered remains of a magical mirror found in the Dreadspire in Hillsfar. Roughly dagger-shaped, the glass is seemingly as hard as steel, making it a weapon of some potency. Additionally, the life-draining magic of the mirror seems to have been retained in the shard itself.
This massive crossbow's name is apt. The amount of force it generates can send a bolt through a brick wall, never mind flesh and bone.

The silver sickles of Soranth are the legendary weapons of a fallen hierophant of Mielikki. Each silver sickle is forged in the shape of a crescent moon. Four pictographs (one on each side of each blade) depict one of the elements killing a wolflike beast. One shows the canine drowning, one shows the canine burning, one shows the canine being crushed under a rock, and one shows the canine gasping for air. The handles are made of duskwood and wrapped in the blackened leather of a werewolf pelt.

Tempus Blackthorne was a powerful wizard and a high-ranking member of the Zhentarim who acted as the personal assistant to the god Bane when he was banished to Faerûn during the Time of Troubles. Despite his evil nature, Blackthorne proved a truly loyal servant of the Black Lord, eventually dying due to a miscast spell while attempting to carry out his master's orders. This staff is all that remains of the vaporized archmage.

These staves are employed primarily by wizards belonging to nefarious organizations such as the Zhentarim, although on occasion a less evil wizard will make use of one when confronted with a particularly unruly student. The staff emits a soft blue glow, and upon striking the target, can cause the simultaneous loss of both sight and hearing for a short time.
This key allows access to the upper floor of the Still Waters Inn.

These powerful staves were originally crafted by a cult of wizard-priests that worshipped Talos. The blackened shafts were taken from mighty oaks toppled during the Storm Lord's frequent rages. The cult then fortified the wood with powerful enchantments and blessed the staff so that the lingering essence of Talos's anger was forever held within.

This awesome weapon once belonged to a solar, the mightiest of the angels that rule the Celestial Planes. It shines a light equivalent to the brightest torch and can slay most enemies in a single blow.
This stone fragment is one quarter of a stone circle forming the symbol of the god Bane: a black, gauntleted fist squeezing four green rays.

Keep an eye on Eremuth - I do not trust him.
